There's a long-running joke that every time Apple unveils a new iPhone Pro, it says it's "the best iPhone we've ever made," as if that were somehow surprising.

Specifically, we expect to see a further step toward that "single piece of glass" vision next year, ending a decade of incremental changes…

The Evolution of the iPhone Pro Lineup

If you line up the iPhone 12 Pro through the 16 Pro, I think most people would struggle to tell them apart at a glance, beyond the shift from the "notch" to the "Dynamic Island" in 2022. The iPhone 17 Pro is only marginally distinguishable, thanks largely to its elongated camera module and Cosmic Orange.

Of course, every generation brings new features, but I'll say this fairly here: unless a particular feature happens to be especially useful to you personally, you really need to skip at least two to three generations before it's worth upgrading for a noticeably better experience.

None of this is a criticism of Apple. The fact is that the smartphone is a mature technology now, at least in terms of conventional design. We don't see huge differences between adjacent generations because there's simply very little left to improve year over year.

Apple is now beginning to experiment with different designs, starting with the iPhone Air, and of course the iPhone Duo—and we expect another significant design leap next year, in the form of a 20th-anniversary model.

Exactly how Apple will position next year's design remains a little unclear. Early rumors suggested it would be a standalone model, separate from the iPhone 19 Pro, but other reports suggest it would be next year's Pro model. There's also the question of whether Apple will use consecutive numbering or skip a number to mark the milestone, so it might end up being called the iPhone 20 Pro.

Personally, I do expect it to be the new iPhone Pro design, whether Apple calls it 19 or 20. If so, the iPhone 18 Pro will be the final iteration of this six- or seven-year-old look.

I'm skipping two generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I'll list separately what's new for me with each yearly model. I'll skip improvements that don't matter to me personally or are completely useless, like going from a 6-core GPU to a 7-core GPU and GenLock.

What's carried over from the iPhone 17 Pro

  • Center Stage front camera for photos and video calls
  • Ultra-stable video
  • Dual-camera simultaneous recording
  • Telephoto lens upgraded from 5x to 8x
  • Telephoto sensor upgraded from 12MP to 48MP
  • ProRes RAW video
  • Better battery life
  • Faster charging speeds

What's new on the iPhone 18 Pro

  • Wider maximum aperture on the main lens
  • Variable aperture on the main lens
  • Pro-grade camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)
  • Third-generation Photographic Styles
  • Smart focus tracking
  • Cinematic effect in standard video
  • Tap-to-zoom and rotate on the front camera
  • Smaller Dynamic Island that can display three Live Activities at once
  • (Even) longer battery life
  • (Even) faster charging speeds

My personal… headline features

For me personally, at this stage, I'm focused on five features.

Variable aperture lens

While the most eye-catching feature is the variable aperture lens, I've said before that we probably shouldn't set our expectations too high for it. The maximum aperture is only marginally wider, and the sensor is still quite small, so I don't expect to see a huge difference in terms of shallow depth-of-field effects.

That said, a wider maximum aperture does let in more light, roughly equivalent to two-thirds of a stop. How much difference that actually makes remains to be seen, but in theory it should mean shorter exposure times for Night mode. Since I use this feature a lot, often handheld, I'm very much looking forward to trying it out.

Pro-grade camera controls

Being able to control shutter speed would certainly be useful for things like tracking shots. Full white balance control would definitely help too. I also expect the histogram to come in very handy when dialing in exposure manually.

I'm generally not a filters person, whether I'm shooting or later editing on the iPhone—I prefer traditional adjustments. So I rarely use the existing Photographic Styles and don't expect to use this latest version much either. But I have to say, I'm genuinely intrigued by its film settings, so I'll definitely give it a try.

One of the biggest weaknesses of autofocus when shooting video is that when a subject is briefly obscured by another object, the camera may shift focus to that obstruction. Smart focus tracking claims to address this, so I'll definitely be putting it through its paces.

Cinematic effect in standard video

Top comment, from atonaldenim

I'm really looking forward to hearing your take once you've spent some time with the 18 Pro. I'm due for an upgrade myself and still using the 12 Mini. (RIP Mini.)

The telephoto would be a nice surprise and might just get me to accept how much heavier and bigger the phone is than the Mini. I'm currently weighing whether to pay the full $1,200 for a new 18 Pro, or grab a used 16 Pro for around $700 or less, which seems to be roughly where they're at right now.

(17 Pro and 18 Pro pricing is still pretty close, so I'm not considering the 17 Pro—I'd rather spend a bit more for the 18 Pro.)

So if you feel that the 18 Pro offers significant improvements over the 16 Pro in the areas you mentioned, I'd really love to hear about it. Thanks!

I said less than two months ago that Apple seemed to have given up on Cinematic video mode. I noted at the time that this was a shame, because if Cinematic mode video were done well, it would be a killer feature for anyone looking to use an iPhone as a more serious video camera. To date, it's been functional, but always missing something; it's always almost there.

But it looks like I was wrong: one of the new features of the iPhone 18 is the ability to apply the Cinematic video effect to standard-mode video.

The convenience of not having to decide in advance whether to use the mode is nice, of course, but what interests me most is that Apple appears to be reinvesting in this feature. It shows they're putting resources behind it, so you can expect it to keep improving, much like Portrait mode did in its early days for stills. I'm really looking forward to testing it.

Those are the features I think might have the biggest impact for me personally. What about you? If you've already upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, which features drove that decision? Feel free to share in the comments.
